messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh Tran is a 52-year-old Vietnamese American HVAC technician, married for twenty-three years, who presented following a toxic chemical exposure incident at a commercial building site approximately eight months ago. He carries a PCL-5 score of 73, reflecting a severe and entrenched symptom picture that has progressively narrowed his world since the event.

The incident occurred on an otherwise routine service call to a large office complex where Minh had been contracted to inspect and repair a rooftop ventilation system. Without adequate warning from the building manager, he entered a mechanical room where a refrigerant line had ruptured overnight, flooding the enclosed space with a high concentration of chemical vapour. Within seconds of entering, Minh experienced a burning sensation in his throat and chest, his vision blurred, and he lost his footing. He recalls the sound of the ventilation ducts humming above him — a sound indistinguishable from any system he services every day — and the sensation of not being able to draw a full breath, convinced in those moments that he was dying alone in a sealed room. A colleague found him on the floor several minutes later. He was hospitalised for three days with chemical bronchitis and discharged with a clean prognosis, but by that point the damage to his sense of safety had already taken root.

In the weeks following discharge, Minh's body did not receive the message that the danger had passed. He described his nervous system as permanently switched on — muscles held tight across his shoulders and jaw from the moment he woke, a low-grade physical vigilance that never fully released. He had come to believe, with a certainty that no reassurance from his pulmonologist or his wife could dislodge, that his body remained in genuine peril, that the chemical had done something that the tests had simply not yet detected. Even when his wife sat beside him and told him he was safe, he found it impossible to believe her. The doctors' words slid off him. He began checking the locks on the doors and windows of their home each evening — once, then again, then a third time — not out of any rational concern about intruders, but because the act of checking gave him a few seconds of something that resembled control over his environment, a brief interruption to the feeling that danger could enter any sealed space without warning.

It was this unrelenting sense of threat that drove the behavioural patterns that have come to define his daily life. Because his body felt perpetually braced for harm, relaxation itself had become suspect — lying still, letting his guard down, felt not like rest but like exposure, like the moment before the chemical hit. He stopped watching television in the evenings, stopped sitting quietly in the garden. At work, the problem became acute: the sound of ductwork, the smell of refrigerant compounds, the sight of a closed mechanical room door — all of it collapsed the present moment back into that humming, burning room. He began declining solo service calls, telling his dispatcher he preferred to work with a partner, and then declining any call that required entering enclosed mechanical spaces alone. Being alone in a room or building had become genuinely intolerable; he needed to know someone else was present and could find him. He avoided anything that might generate additional stress — conflict, deadlines, unfamiliar environments — as though his system had calculated, correctly from its own distorted logic, that it had no remaining capacity to absorb further threat. His employer, initially accommodating, has grown frustrated. Minh has turned down enough assignments that his hours have been quietly reduced, and he is aware the situation is unsustainable.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment last month when he sat in his truck outside a client's building for forty minutes, unable to make himself go in, and then drove home without calling his dispatcher. He told his wife that evening, for the first time, that he was frightened not of the building but of himself — of how small his life had become. What he hopes for, tentatively, is to be able to work again without terror. What he fears most is that the tightness in his chest means the danger was never over.
